title: Climbing On Autopilot
author: Andrea Chiarelli
source: theartofaskingquestions.com (The Art of Asking Questions), October 4, 2026
summary: Andrea Chiarelli argues that many people pursue promotions on autopilot, with a ready career story but no clear reason why the path has gone the way it has. He says the usual scorecard of money, position and prestige leaves out time, the one resource that cannot be replenished, and he uses Jensen Huang's blunt answer that he would not build NVIDIA again knowing the cost as a reminder that climbing has trade-offs. He explains how deferred plans, from family time to the book never written, lose to the clearly priced cost of stepping sideways. Drawing on self-determination theory, he says status and approval satisfy autonomy, competence and relatedness less well than chosen goals, and that targets reset through the ratchet effect and the hedonic treadmill. He concludes that organizations can build cultures of examined ambition, but the individual must re-justify the climb at every rung because nobody upstream runs the motive check.
points: The common career scorecard ignores time, so each rung is paid for with something that cannot be recovered, and even NVIDIA's Jensen Huang says he would not repeat the climb.
Phrases like 'the natural next step' are usually cover stories for status, safety or external validation that were never tested against what the role demands.
Self-determination theory suggests autonomy, competence and relatedness sustain motivation, while extrinsic goals pursued for their own sake leave the climber unsatisfied.
The ratchet effect and the hedonic treadmill together mean that hitting a target resets the definition of enough both inside the organization and inside the person.
Promotion decisions check readiness, not motive, so the individual must ask why they want the job before accepting the next rung.
quotes: Because we tend to have a career story ready, but we less often have a clear reason why our career has gone that way.

Most career advice is about acceleration and continuous progress: how to get promoted faster, and how to close the distance between where you are and where you want to be. But that framing doesn’t examine what “getting there” actually costs.
The reason we keep deferring our desires is that career progress has a price tag attached. You can put a number on what you’d lose by stepping sideways or slowing down.
The result is a system where capable people conclude, again and again, that they can’t afford to do the things they’re working so hard to eventually afford.
That persistence is itself evidence. If the climbing were really about arriving, arriving would be enough to stop it.

Between the two effects, the leader is squeezed from both directions: the organisation keeps raising what it expects, and the leader’s own sense of achievement keeps requiring more to register at all.
A promotion decision is almost always a readiness check (can this person do the job?), and tends to miss the motive check asking whether that person should want the job, and why.
So you should re-justify the climb to yourself at every rung. Your manager can ask the question, and a good organisation can make space for it, but the thinking is yours alone.
